It ships with a 400K token context window (272K input, 128K output), API pricing of $1.25 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and scored around 90 on MMLU alongside strong marks on coding and agentic benchmarks at launch. OpenAI framed it as a jump in reliability and reduced hallucination rate rather than a dramatic leap in raw capability, positioning it against Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro and Anthropic’s Claude models of the same era. By mid-2026 OpenAI had already iterated past it with the GPT-5.x line, including the GPT-5.6 family, but GPT-5 remains available in the API and ChatGPT.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Luna
item.description: GPT-5.6 Luna is the fast, low-cost tier of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 family, which began a limited government-vetted preview in late June 2026 before opening to the wider public on July 9, 2026 once the US Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation cleared broader access. Luna is built for summarization, drafting, and high-volume automation where speed and cost matter more than maximum reasoning depth, and it shares the family’s 1.05 million token context window with support for up to 128,000 output tokens. At $1 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, it undercuts the mid-tier Terra model by a wide margin while still handling everyday chat and lightweight coding tasks. OpenAI pitched the three-tier Sol, Terra, Luna structure as a way for developers to trade off cost against capability without switching model families, following the same pattern it used with the GPT-5 mini and nano tiers.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Sol
item.description: GPT-5.6 Sol is OpenAI’s flagship model in the GPT-5.6 family, built for frontier reasoning, complex coding, multi-step agentic work, and cybersecurity research. OpenAI first shipped it as a locked-down preview to a small group of US-government-vetted organizations in late June 2026, then opened it to the public on July 9, 2026 after regulatory review cleared wider access. It carries the family’s 1.05 million token context window and 128,000 token output limit, priced at $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens, the highest tier of the three. OpenAI says Sol launched with its most extensive safety stack yet, adding tighter controls around sensitive cyber-related requests and repeated misuse attempts given its stronger offensive and defensive security capabilities. Rather than reporting the older MMLU-style academic scores, OpenAI emphasized agentic and practical benchmarks for this release, a shift several independent reviewers noted as a departure from prior GPT-5.x announcements.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Terra
item.description: GPT-5.6 Terra is the balanced, middle tier of OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 family, aimed at everyday coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks where Sol’s top-end capability would be overkill. It reached the public on July 9, 2026, following a preview period restricted to organizations vetted by the US government, and shares the family’s 1.05 million token context window and 128,000 token output cap. OpenAI prices it at $2.50 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, roughly half the cost of Sol, and describes its performance as competitive with the prior GPT-5.5 generation at that lower price. Terra is meant to be the default choice for developers who need strong reasoning and coding ability without paying flagship rates, similar to the role GPT-5’s mini tier played in the previous generation. It is available through ChatGPT, Azure OpenAI, and the standard API, and GitHub added it to Copilot the same day it launched.

item.title: GPT-Image-1
item.description: GPT-Image-1 is OpenAI’s native multimodal image generation model, the technology behind the image generator built into ChatGPT and offered separately through the Images API since April 23, 2025. Unlike the DALL-E series, which used a diffusion process, GPT-Image-1 generates images autoregressively within the same architecture family as OpenAI’s language models, which is why it follows detailed instructions and renders legible text inside images noticeably better than its predecessors. It supports text-to-image generation and editing at three quality tiers and three resolutions, including square, portrait, and landscape formats, with per-image pricing that scales from roughly a cent to about a quarter of a dollar depending on quality and size. It competes directly with Google’s Imagen and Midjourney for prompt-following and text rendering, and it has been widely adopted by developers building design and marketing tools on top of the API. OpenAI has already moved on to GPT-Image-1.5 and newer versions, and has set an October 23, 2026 deprecation date for the original GPT-Image-1 endpoint.

item.title: GPT-OSS-120B
item.description: GPT-OSS-120B is an open-weight reasoning model OpenAI released on August 5, 2025, marking its first open model release since GPT-2 in 2019. It uses a mixture-of-experts transformer architecture with 117 billion total parameters but only about 5.1 billion active per token, which lets it run reasoning-heavy workloads on a single high-end GPU instead of the multi-GPU clusters dense models of similar size would need. It scored around 90 on MMLU at launch, putting it in the same range as OpenAI’s own o4-mini on many reasoning and coding benchmarks, and it ships under the Apache 2.0 license so companies can self-host it, fine-tune it, and run it without usage restrictions. OpenAI built it specifically to compete with open releases from Meta, Mistral, and Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Alibaba’s Qwen team, which had been setting the pace in open-weight models while OpenAI stayed closed. It is available through Hugging Face, Together AI, Azure AI Foundry, and OpenAI’s own API for organizations that want the option of both open self-hosting and managed hosting.

item.title: GPT-OSS-20B
item.description: GPT-OSS-20B is the smaller of the two open-weight models OpenAI released on August 5, 2025, alongside the larger GPT-OSS-120B, in its first open model release since GPT-2. It uses a mixture-of-experts design with about 21 billion total parameters and roughly 3.6 billion active per token, light enough to run on a single consumer GPU with 16GB or more of memory, which was the point: OpenAI built it for developers and hobbyists who wanted a capable reasoning model without server-grade hardware. It scored 85.3 on MMLU at launch, a strong result for its size class, and handles coding, math, and general reasoning tasks reasonably close to its bigger sibling despite the much smaller footprint. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, it can be fine-tuned and redistributed freely, and it is available through Hugging Face, Together AI, and OpenAI’s API for teams that want a managed option instead of self-hosting.

item.title: Granite 13B
item.description: Granite 13B is one of IBM’s first foundation models built for its watsonx enterprise AI platform, announced on September 7, 2023 alongside a family of Granite models aimed at business use cases rather than general chat. It has 13 billion parameters, uses multi-query attention with learned position embeddings, and was trained with the tokenizer from EleutherAI’s GPT-NeoX-20B, giving it an 8,192 token context window. IBM built it for tasks like document summarization, question answering, and text classification inside regulated industries such as banking and insurance, and it came with IBM’s standard indemnification for customers worried about training-data copyright exposure, a selling point competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic did not offer at the time. Granite 13B was proprietary and accessible only through watsonx, distinguishing it from IBM’s later Granite 3 generation, which shifted toward openly licensed weights on Hugging Face. It has since been superseded by newer Granite versions as IBM’s enterprise AI lineup moved toward open weights and broader benchmark parity with mainstream models.

item.title: Grok 3
item.description: Grok 3 is xAI’s model released on February 17, 2025, trained on the Colossus supercomputer in Memphis using more than 200,000 GPUs, roughly ten times the compute xAI put into Grok-2. xAI pitched it as a reasoning model with a “Think” mode that can spend anywhere from seconds to minutes working through a problem, checking its own steps and backtracking before answering, and it reported an Elo score of 1402 on Chatbot Arena along with strong results on GPQA, AIME math competition problems, and MMLU-Pro. The context window grew to 1 million tokens, eight times what earlier Grok models supported, letting it handle much longer documents and codebases in one request. Grok 3 is priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens through xAI’s API, and it’s also available through the Grok app and X. xAI positioned it against OpenAI’s o3, Gemini 2 Pro, and DeepSeek V3, claiming an edge in math and science reasoning at launch.

item.title: Grok 4
item.description: Grok 4 is xAI’s flagship model released on July 9, 2025, positioned as a reasoning-first successor to Grok 3 with heavier test-time compute and a redesigned training pipeline. At launch, Artificial Analysis measured it at the top of its Intelligence Index, ahead of OpenAI’s o3 and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro at the time, and xAI reported an all-time-high GPQA Diamond score near 88 percent along with a joint-best AIME 2024 score around 94 percent. It supports a 256,000-token context window and handles both text and images, and xAI made it available through the Grok app, X, and the API at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Grok 4’s launch drew attention beyond benchmarks too, including scrutiny over some of its unfiltered responses on X, which xAI addressed with follow-up moderation changes. It set the baseline that xAI’s later Grok 4 Fast and Grok 4.5 releases built on through 2025 and 2026.

item.title: Grok 4 Fast
item.description: Grok 4 Fast is xAI’s cost- and latency-optimized tier of Grok 4, released September 19, 2025 for high-volume use cases like customer support, search, and agentic tool calling where running the full Grok 4 model on every request would be too slow or expensive. Despite the “fast” branding, it keeps a large 2-million-token context window and ships in both reasoning and non-reasoning variants so developers can pick the latency profile they need. Pricing is aggressive at $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, undercutting most other frontier-adjacent models on a cost basis while still drawing on the same underlying Grok 4 training. xAI markets it heavily on agentic benchmarks and tool-use tasks rather than raw knowledge tests, and it’s available only through the API rather than the consumer Grok app or X.

item.title: Grok 4.5
item.description: Grok 4.5 is xAI’s model released on July 8, 2026, built with a heavier emphasis on coding, agentic workflows, and knowledge work than earlier Grok releases. On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scored 54, placing fourth overall among frontier models while taking the top spot specifically on agentic tool use, and it posted 83.3 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 64.7 percent on SWE-Bench Pro, both benchmarks aimed at real coding and terminal tasks rather than multiple-choice knowledge tests. It carries a 1-million-token context window and handles text and image input, and xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, with a cheaper $0.50 rate for cached input tokens. It’s reachable through the xAI API console, the Grok app, X, and a wide set of third-party integrations including Cursor, OpenRouter, Vercel, and Microsoft’s Word, Excel, and PowerPoint add-ins. Some coverage framed it as xAI’s answer to Anthropic’s Opus-class models, given the shared focus on long agentic coding sessions.

item.title: Grok-2
item.description: Grok-2 is xAI’s model released in beta on August 13, 2024, alongside a smaller Grok-2 mini variant. It was the first Grok model to reach a wide audience with both image understanding and native image generation, the latter built on a partnership with Black Forest Labs’ Flux model, and it integrates directly with X for access to real-time posts and trends. On released benchmarks, xAI reported an MMLU score around 87.5 percent along with strong results on GPQA, MATH, and document visual question answering, putting it roughly in line with GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro class models at the time. Grok-2 is available through X, the standalone Grok app, and xAI’s API at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. It remained xAI’s flagship offering until Grok 3 arrived in February 2025, and a later Grok-2 checkpoint (Grok-2-1212) continued to see API use even after that.

item.title: GTE-large
item.description: GTE-large is a text embedding model from Alibaba DAMO Academy, published on Hugging Face in mid-2023 as part of the General Text Embeddings (GTE) family alongside smaller GTE-base and GTE-small variants. It’s a 335-million-parameter BERT-style encoder trained with multi-stage contrastive learning on a broad mix of web and domain text, producing 1024-dimension vectors from inputs up to 512 tokens. The model is meant for retrieval, semantic search, clustering, and reranking, and at release it scored well on the MTEB benchmark leaderboard relative to other open embedding models of similar size, competing directly with BGE and E5 style models from other Chinese labs. GTE-large is open-weighted under Apache 2.0, runs easily on a single GPU or CPU for inference, and is distributed through Hugging Face and Alibaba Cloud, making it a common default choice for teams building RAG pipelines who want a compact embedding model without an API dependency.

item.title: Hunyuan DiT
item.description: Hunyuan-DiT is Tencent’s open-weight text-to-image model, built on a diffusion transformer architecture rather than the U-Net design most earlier diffusion models used. Tencent published it in May 2024, pairing a 1.5B-parameter denoising transformer with bilingual CLIP and multilingual T5 text encoders so it can follow prompts written in Chinese or English with similar fidelity. That bilingual focus is the model’s main selling point: most open text-to-image models of the time handled Chinese prompts poorly, and Hunyuan-DiT was trained specifically to close that gap. It generates 1024x1024 images and includes a built-in multimodal chat component that lets users refine an image across several turns of dialogue instead of rewriting the whole prompt each time. Tencent released the weights on Hugging Face and GitHub under its Hunyuan license, and later shipped a 1.1 update that fixed oversaturation and watermark artifacts present in the original checkpoint.

item.title: Hunyuan Turbo
item.description: Hunyuan Turbo is Tencent’s production-tier large language model, offered as an API-only service through Tencent Cloud rather than as open weights. Tencent positioned it as the fast, lower-cost counterpart to its larger flagship Hunyuan models, aimed at applications that need quick responses at scale, such as chat products and customer service bots built on WeChat and other Tencent platforms. The company has not disclosed the parameter count, consistent with how it handles its other proprietary API tiers, but has published pricing and periodically cut rates as it iterated toward successor tiers like Hunyuan Turbo S. It supports a 128K context window and is aimed at developers who want Hunyuan-family quality without paying for or waiting on the largest model in the lineup. Its main competition comes from other Chinese low-latency API tiers, including Alibaba’s Qwen-Turbo and Baidu’s ERNIE Speed.

item.title: Hunyuan3D
item.description: Hunyuan3D is Tencent’s open-weight system for turning text prompts or reference images into 3D assets, with the widely used 2.0 release published in January 2025. It splits the job into two models: a 2.6B-parameter shape generator built on a flow-based diffusion transformer that produces an untextured mesh, and a 1.3B-parameter texture model that paints high-resolution PBR materials onto that mesh afterward. That two-stage split lets each part specialize, so the shape model focuses purely on geometry while the texture model handles color, lighting response, and surface detail. Tencent released the weights on Hugging Face and GitHub under its Hunyuan license, giving game studios and 3D artists a way to run asset generation locally instead of through a paid API. It competes with other open and semi-open 3D generators such as TripoSR and Stability AI’s TripoSG, and later Hunyuan3D versions (2.1, 2.5) pushed texture fidelity and geometry detail further.

item.title: HyperCLOVA X
item.description: HyperCLOVA X is Naver’s flagship large language model, unveiled in August 2023 as South Korea’s answer to GPT-4 and one of the first major foundation models trained with a heavy emphasis on Korean language and cultural context rather than English-first data. Naver has said the model runs on roughly 204 billion parameters, more than GPT-3’s 175 billion, though the company has since focused on making later variants smaller and more efficient rather than simply larger. It powers Naver’s CLOVA X chat assistant and is available to businesses through Naver Cloud’s API, where it competes with global models on Korean-specific tasks like local search, e-commerce, and customer service where dialect, honorifics, and cultural references matter. Naver has followed the original release with specialized variants, including HyperCLOVA X Vision for image understanding and HyperCLOVA X THINK, a reasoning-focused version with an expanded context window. The strategy reflects a broader pattern of national or regional players building models tuned to a specific language market rather than competing head-on with OpenAI or Google on general capability alone.

item.title: HyperCLOVA X Vision
item.description: HyperCLOVA X Vision is Naver’s multimodal extension of its HyperCLOVA X language model, adding image understanding on top of the text model’s Korean-language strength. Naver introduced it in August 2024, and the company has said it answered 83.8 percent of Korean college entrance exam questions that included image inputs, ahead of the 77.8 percent Naver reported for GPT-4o on the same test. That benchmark matters for Naver’s pitch: rather than compete on generic multimodal leaderboards, the model is built to handle Korean-specific documents, exam questions, and visual context that Western models tend to get wrong. It’s available through Naver Cloud’s API and the CLOVA X app, aimed at Korean enterprises that need document QA, chart reading, or image-grounded chat in their own language. Naver has continued to expand the lineup with smaller open variants under the HyperCLOVA X SEED family and an omnimodal version that adds audio.

item.title: Ideogram 1.0
item.description: Ideogram 1.0 is the debut text-to-image model from Ideogram, a startup founded by ex-Google Brain researchers, released in February 2024 alongside an $80 million Series A round. Its standout feature at launch was legible in-image text: at the time, most diffusion models scrambled letters and words badly enough that adding readable text to a generated image was mostly a losing bet. Ideogram claimed roughly half the text-rendering error rate of competing models on its own evaluations, which made the model useful for things earlier tools struggled with, like posters, T-shirt designs, memes, and logos with real words in them. The model also shipped with Magic Prompt, a built-in prompt-expansion feature that fleshes out short user inputs into more detailed prompts before generation. Ideogram has since moved past 1.0 with 2.0 and 3.0 releases that pushed further on photorealism and typography, but 1.0 is the release that established text rendering as the company’s core differentiator against Midjourney and DALL-E.

item.title: Ideogram 2.0
item.description: Ideogram 2.0 is Ideogram’s second-generation text-to-image model, launched on August 21, 2024 and made free to all users on release day. It added five selectable style presets (regular, realistic, design, 3D, and anime), noticeably better rendering of hands, eyes, and skin in the realistic style, and color palette controls that let users lock a generation to specific brand or mood colors. The same launch introduced Ideogram Search, letting users browse over a billion public generations for inspiration, along with a new iOS app and a beta public API. Where Ideogram 1.0 was mainly known for solving legible in-image text, 2.0 broadened the pitch toward general image quality and stylistic control while keeping that typography advantage intact. It positioned Ideogram as a more complete competitor to Midjourney rather than a niche tool for text-heavy graphics alone.

item.title: Ideogram 3.0
item.description: Ideogram 3.0 is Ideogram’s third-generation image model, released on March 26, 2025 with sharper photorealism and a text-rendering accuracy that independent testing put around 90 percent, well ahead of the roughly 30 percent seen on Midjourney for similar short phrases. It introduced Style References, which let users upload a reference image and carry its visual style into new generations, plus Magic Fill and Extend, inpainting and outpainting tools built into Ideogram’s Canvas editor. Batch generation at scale is gated to paid plans, reflecting how Ideogram has increasingly split free and pro tiers by production-scale features rather than just image quality. API pricing lands around six cents per image, keeping it in a similar range to other commercial text-to-image APIs. The release keeps typography as Ideogram’s signature strength while catching up on editing tools that competitors like Midjourney and Adobe Firefly had already built out.

item.title: Imagen 2
item.description: Imagen 2 is Google DeepMind’s second-generation text-to-image model, previewed at Google I/O in May 2023 and made generally available on Vertex AI in December 2023. It improved photorealism and added logo and text rendering, an area where the original Imagen and most contemporaries were noticeably weak. Google positioned it as an enterprise-ready image model rather than a consumer toy, shipping it through Vertex AI with the customization tooling, managed infrastructure, and safety filtering that business customers expect from a cloud platform product. It later gained a short video-clip generation mode inside Vertex AI. Imagen 2 sat in Google’s lineup between the original Imagen research model and the more capable Imagen 3, which replaced it as Google’s primary image model through 2024.

item.title: Imagen 3
item.description: Imagen 3 is Google DeepMind’s third-generation text-to-image model, opened to Gemini and ImageFX users in August 2024. It improved on Imagen 2 in prompt understanding, image detail, and text rendering across multiple languages and scripts, and it supports five aspect ratios so users aren’t stuck with square output by default. Google rolled it out gradually, first to Gemini Advanced, Business, and Enterprise users before wider access, partly to phase in safeguards around generating images of real people. It’s available through Vertex AI for developers and through the Gemini app for consumers, putting it in direct competition with OpenAI’s DALL-E 3 and Midjourney on general-purpose image quality. Google later replaced it with Imagen 4 as its flagship image model, but Imagen 3 remained Google’s main text-to-image offering for roughly a year.

item.title: Imagen 4
item.description: Imagen 4 is Google DeepMind’s text-to-image model, announced at Google I/O in May 2025 and made generally available through the Gemini API and Vertex AI. It generates images at resolutions up to 2K and renders legible text and typography inside images, an area where earlier Imagen versions and many competing models struggled. Google ships it as a family of three variants: a fast tier built for quick drafts at roughly ten times the speed of Imagen 3, a standard tier, and an Ultra tier for maximum fidelity and prompt adherence. Pricing is per image and tiered by variant, with the fast option priced lowest and Ultra priced highest.

item.title: Jina Embeddings v2
item.description: Jina Embeddings v2 is a text embedding model from Jina AI, released in October 2023. It came in two main sizes, a 33 million parameter small version and a 137 million parameter base version, both built on a modified BERT architecture using ALiBi position encoding instead of standard positional embeddings. That choice let it handle sequences up to 8,192 tokens, which was unusual for an open embedding model at the time and let it compete with OpenAI’s proprietary text-embedding-ada-002 on long document retrieval while being far smaller. The model is released under an Apache 2.0 license and can be run locally or accessed through Jina’s API. It has since been superseded by jina-embeddings-v3, which adds multilingual support and task-specific adapters, but v2 remains in use for English-language retrieval tasks where its smaller size is an advantage.

item.title: Kimi K1.5
item.description: Kimi K1.5 is Moonshot AI’s first reasoning-focused model, released in January 2025 as the company’s answer to OpenAI’s o1. It is trained with reinforcement learning on long chains of thought and can reason jointly over text and images, which let Moonshot claim results on par with o1 on math, coding, and multimodal benchmarks like MathVista, AIME, and Codeforces. The model supports a 128,000-token context window and includes a “long2short” technique that transfers reasoning gains from long chains of thought into shorter, faster responses for everyday queries. Moonshot has not disclosed the parameter count. K1.5 was Moonshot’s proof that a Chinese lab could compete at the reasoning frontier, and it set the stage for the open-weight Kimi K2 line that followed a few months later.

item.title: Kimi-Audio
item.description: Kimi-Audio is an open-weight audio foundation model from Moonshot AI, with pretrained and instruction-tuned 7B checkpoints released in late April 2025. It handles speech recognition, audio understanding, and speech generation in a single model, so it can transcribe audio, answer questions about a sound clip, and produce spoken output rather than needing separate models stitched together. Moonshot released the model along with an evaluation toolkit, and the weights and code are on GitHub and Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license. It sits alongside Kimi-VL and the Kimi K-series text models in Moonshot’s push to open-source specialized components rather than keep every capability behind a closed API, and it gives developers a free, self-hostable alternative to commercial speech models like OpenAI’s Whisper and Google’s audio models.

item.title: Kling 2.0
item.description: Kling 2.0 is Kuaishou’s video generation model, launched in April 2025 at the company’s “Inspiration Comes True” event alongside a matching image model, Ketu 2.0. It takes text prompts or reference images and turns them into video, and Kuaishou focused the upgrade on smoother, more natural motion after earlier Kling versions drew criticism for stiff or jerky animation. The Master Edition adds a multimodal video editing feature that lets users add, remove, or replace elements in an existing generated clip by feeding in new text or images, rather than starting a generation over from scratch. Kuaishou positions Kling as a direct competitor to Runway, Pika, and Sora, and the 2.0 release was aimed at closing the gap on complex prompts, camera movement, and visual consistency across a shot. Kuaishou has continued iterating quickly since, with 2.1, 2.6, and 3.0 following within about a year.

item.title: Kolors
item.description: Kolors is Kuaishou’s open-weight text-to-image model, released in July 2024. It is a latent diffusion model with about 2.6 billion parameters, built on a U-Net architecture, and it uses ChatGLM as its text encoder instead of a CLIP-style encoder, which gives it a notable edge at reading and rendering Chinese-language prompts and Chinese text within images. It generates at a native 1024x1024 resolution and supports multiple aspect ratios. Kuaishou trained it on billions of text-image pairs and released the weights on GitHub and Hugging Face, free for research use, with a separate registration process required for commercial deployment. Alongside models like Flux and Stable Diffusion 3, Kolors is one of the few widely-used open image models that handles non-Latin scripts well.

item.title: Leonardo Diffusion XL
item.description: Leonardo Diffusion XL is one of Leonardo AI’s earlier in-house models, a fine-tune built on Stability AI’s Stable Diffusion XL architecture rather than a model trained from scratch. It was tuned to produce strong results from short, simple prompts, which made it a popular default for users who did not want to write long descriptive prompts to get usable output. It covers a broad range of styles, from photography to illustration, and became one of the more widely used models on the Leonardo platform before the company shipped its own foundational model, Phoenix, at the end of 2024. Leonardo AI, founded in Sydney in 2022, was acquired by Canva in July 2024, and Diffusion XL is now maintained mainly for users with existing workflows built around it rather than promoted as the platform’s leading option.

item.title: Leonardo Phoenix
item.description: Leonardo Phoenix is Leonardo AI’s first foundational image model trained in-house rather than fine-tuned from a third-party base, launched December 18, 2024 alongside Flux Dev and Flux Schnell support on the platform. Leonardo built it specifically to close the prompt-adherence gap with competitors: it follows long, detailed instructions closely and can render short strings of coherent text inside an image, a common weak spot for diffusion models of that era. It works across a wide range of styles at high fidelity and is available through both the Leonardo app and API, positioning it against models like Midjourney and DALL-E for creators who need precise control over output rather than loose interpretation of a prompt. Leonardo followed it with Phoenix 2.0 in late 2025, which added a consistent-character engine, faster generation, and basic image-to-video motion, building on the same foundation this original model established.

item.title: Llama 3.1 70B
item.description: Llama 3.1 70B is the middle tier of Meta’s July 2024 Llama 3.1 release, sitting between the 8 billion parameter version and the 405 billion parameter flagship. Meta trained the whole family on more than 15 trillion tokens and extended the context window to 128,000 tokens, a big jump from the 8,192 tokens of the original Llama 3. The 70B model added multilingual support and better tool use, and on benchmarks like MMLU and HumanEval it lands close to the far larger 405B model at a fraction of the compute cost. Because Meta released the weights openly under the Llama 3.1 Community License, the 70B tier became a common choice for companies that wanted strong quality they could self-host or run through third-party API providers such as Together AI and AWS Bedrock.

item.title: Luma Dream Machine 1.0
item.description: Luma Dream Machine 1.0 is Luma AI’s first publicly available video generation model, launched in June 2024 as a free web tool that turns text prompts or a starting image into short video clips. It generates roughly five-second shots and was notable at launch for handling physics and motion more convincingly than most competing video models at the time, keeping characters and objects consistent as they move rather than warping between frames. Luma built it as a large-scale generative transformer trained directly on video and text, distinct from the diffusion-based approaches several rivals used. The tool grew quickly after launch, reportedly passing 25 million registered users, and it made Luma one of the more visible names in AI video generation alongside Runway and Pika.

item.title: Luma Photon
item.description: Luma Photon is Luma AI’s image generation model, launched in November 2024 as a companion to its Dream Machine video tools. It is built on the same underlying multimodal architecture Luma uses for video, which the company says lets it render more consistent characters, scenes, and camera-like framing than typical diffusion-based image generators. Photon shipped alongside a faster, cheaper variant called Photon Flash, with API pricing around $0.015 per 1080p image for the full model and a fraction of that for Flash. Luma positioned Photon as a low-cost, high-throughput option for creative and marketing teams generating large volumes of images through its API or the Dream Machine app.

item.title: Luma Ray 3
item.description: Luma Ray 3 is Luma AI’s flagship video generation model, released in September 2025 as what the company calls the first reasoning video model. Rather than generating pixels directly from a prompt, Ray 3 produces both text and visual tokens as it works, planning a scene and checking its own output before finalizing a clip, similar to a director sketching a storyboard before shooting. It is also the first video model to output true 10, 12, and 16-bit HDR footage in ACES2065-1 EXR format, aimed at professional film and advertising pipelines rather than just social clips. A Draft Mode lets users generate many quick low-cost variations before committing to a final high-resolution HDR render, and Adobe added Ray 3 to Firefly shortly after launch, giving it a route into mainstream creative software.

item.title: Luminous
item.description: Luminous is a family of large language models from the German company Aleph Alpha, first released in April 2022 in three sizes: Luminous Base, Extended, and Supreme, with the largest Supreme tier reaching 70 billion parameters by that August. Aleph Alpha built Luminous as a multilingual model with an early focus on European languages and enterprise use cases where regulatory compliance and data residency in the EU matter. Its most distinctive feature is explainability: Luminous can point back to the specific passages in its input that a given output was based on, a source-attribution capability aimed at industries like law, finance, and government that need to audit AI-generated answers. Aleph Alpha positions Luminous as a European alternative to US-based models from OpenAI and Google, sold mainly to enterprise and public-sector customers through its own API rather than to general consumers.

item.title: Lyria
item.description: Lyria is Google DeepMind’s music generation model, built to turn text prompts into produced audio tracks. The version available through Vertex AI (Lyria 2) generates instrumental music from text descriptions, handling a wide range of genres and picking up on the texture of individual instruments, while the streaming variant, Lyria RealTime, produces continuous music over a WebSocket connection that responds to live parameter changes. DeepMind pairs every clip with a SynthID watermark so the audio can be identified as AI-generated after the fact.

item.title: Mistral Embed
item.description:
Mistral Embed is Mistral AI’s text embedding model, available through its API since early 2024, that converts text into 1024-dimensional vectors for semantic search, clustering, and retrieval-augmented generation. It accepts inputs up to 8,192 tokens and Mistral positions it as a general-purpose embedding option for teams already building on the Mistral platform, rather than a specialized model for code or multilingual retrieval.

It is priced at $0.01 per million input tokens, making it one of the cheaper hosted embedding options available, and is accessed exclusively through Mistral’s API rather than as downloadable weights. Mistral later added Codestral Embed, a separate model tuned specifically for code retrieval, leaving Mistral Embed as the general-text option in its lineup.

item.title: Mistral Large 2
item.description: Mistral Large 2 is a 123 billion parameter dense language model that Mistral AI released on July 24, 2024, replacing the original Mistral Large as the company’s flagship offering. It handles a 128,000-token context window, scores 84.0% on MMLU, and Mistral trained it with heavy emphasis on multilingual ability, covering languages including French, German, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, and Hindi alongside English, plus more than 80 programming languages for code generation.

item.title: Mistral Large 3
item.description: Mistral Large 3 is Mistral AI’s flagship language model, released on December 2, 2025 as part of the broader Mistral 3 lineup. It uses a sparse mixture-of-experts design with 675 billion total parameters but only about 41 billion active per token, so it runs at roughly the compute cost of a much smaller dense model while drawing on a far larger pool of learned weights. It takes both text and images as input, handles a 256,000-token context window, and Mistral released the weights under an Apache 2.0 license, a departure from the closed approach it took with Mistral Large 2.
